title: US oil production starts to respond to higher prices | Wood Mackenzie
gist: Wood Mackenzie argues US Lower 48 oil output, up only about 60,000 b/d since the Iran war began, is just starting to respond to higher prices with a 9-12 month lag, and now forecasts about 11.8 million b/d by December 2027, 1 million b/d above its pre-war view. Volatility and backwardation restrain disciplined majors, so the US is a delayed rather than immediate swing producer.

themes.theme: US energy security illusions shattered by Iran war

insights.claim: The war with Iran has shown that US integration into global crude and product markets means Middle East disruption still hits American consumers directly, undermining 2010s claims that tight oil made the US indifferent to the region and the SPR obsolete.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: US producer status does not insulate domestic fuel prices; global tightness transmits straight to pump prices and politics.
insights.quote: The unfolding crisis created by the war with Iran has shattered those illusions.
insights.locator: When the US tight oil industry emerged in the 2010s

insights.claim: US retail gasoline averages about $4.36 a gallon, up 41% year on year, and diesel about $6.28, up 71%, per AAA.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Diesel's outsized rise signals a middle-distillate squeeze that feeds freight, farm and inflation pressure.
insights.locator: The average retail price of regular gasoline in the US

insights.claim: As a net oil exporter the US benefits overall from higher prices, but gains accrue to producers while consumers lose, so the impact is uneven, and consumers have yet to see any offsetting benefit from a US supply surge.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Political pressure for export curbs or other interventions rises when consumers bear costs without supply relief.
insights.locator: In the longer term, being a net oil exporter

themes.theme: Diesel supply, Russia sanctions relief and SPR

insights.claim: President Trump announced Russia would partially lift its July diesel export ban in return for sanctions relief, with about 800,000 tons (roughly 120,000 b/d) sold in October and November and another 1 million tons soon after.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Sanctions relief is being traded for distillate supply, a precedent that can ease diesel cracks but weakens the sanctions regime.
insights.locator: The importance of global supplies for US consumers was underlined on Friday

insights.claim: Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have disrupted global diesel supplies, and Trump told Zelenskyy to end them, tying US consumer prices to the Russia-Ukraine battlefield.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Refinery strikes are a diesel price risk factor, and US pressure to stop them could ease product tightness.
insights.locator: Over the weekend, President Trump told President Volodymyr Zelenskyy

insights.claim: About 132 million barrels have been released from the US SPR since March at roughly 630,000 b/d, with a planned total of 172 million barrels structured as an exchange to be repaid with interest, plus 4 million more for Hurricane Isaias.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: SPR repayment with interest creates future deferred demand, supporting back-end prices once the crisis eases.
insights.locator: Meanwhile,the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve

insights.claim: US Lower 48 crude and condensate output is expected at about 11.35 million b/d this month versus 11.29 million b/d in February before the war, a rise of only about 60,000 b/d, so US upstream's contribution to extra global supply has been negligible so far.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: The supply response has not yet capped prices, leaving the market dependent on SPR and other releases near term.
insights.locator: In February, just before the war began

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's rule of thumb is that US production takes nine to 12 months to respond to price moves, so the first increases from the late-February price surge are only now appearing.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Use the 9-12 month lag to time expectations of US supply growth and the resulting downward pressure on prices.
insights.locator: Wood Mackenzie's rule of thumb is that production typically takes

insights.claim: Treating US tight oil as an instant swing producer is a fallacy because output reflects hundreds of independent company decisions, there is no spare capacity reserve, and firms raise output only if it maximises shareholder value; yet assuming no response is the opposite error.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Neither a quick price-capping supply response nor stagnation should be priced in; the response is delayed but real.
insights.quote: two opposite fallacies that people can fall into
insights.locator: When thinking about how the US oil industry will respond

insights.claim: The lag stems from mobilising rigs and pressure pumping fleets, drilling, fracking and bringing wells online, compounded by price volatility that deters spending because wells might come on stream after prices have fallen back.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Oilfield services demand lags price spikes and depends on how long prices are perceived to stay high.
insights.locator: There are several factors behind that lag

insights.claim: Extreme price volatility makes producers cautious, with one Wood Mackenzie analyst noting a single tweet can move crude by $20 a barrel and a Dallas Fed survey respondent saying swings of $5, $10 and $20 make choosing a planning price very hard.
insights.speaker: Nathan Nemeth, quoted by Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: High volatility suppresses the capex response, prolonging elevated prices relative to a calm market.
insights.quote: One tweet can drop crude by US$20 a barrel.
insights.locator: A volatile environment, where the oil price outlook is highly uncertain

insights.claim: A futures market in steep backwardation for much of this year, with prompt prices well above those six to twelve months out, makes it hard to hedge, further discouraging added drilling.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Backwardation signals the market expects prices to fall, and it blunts producers' incentive to lock in growth economics.
insights.locator: An oil futures market in steep backwardation

insights.claim: Majors and larger independents, whose appeal rests on disciplined capital and reliable dividends, are most reluctant to raise spending, while smaller and private operators are the ones ramping up, with US oil rigs at 462 versus 418 a year ago per Baker Hughes.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Growth is coming from private and small-cap E&Ps, not from large listed names, which shapes who captures upside.
insights.locator: The oil Majors and larger independents

themes.theme: Wood Mackenzie production and price outlook

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie raised its December 2026 Lower 48 forecast from close to 11 million b/d to about 11.4 million b/d, and projects about 11.8 million b/d by December 2027, a full 1 million b/d above its pre-war forecast.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: A material 2027 US supply increase is a bearish factor for oil prices beyond the near term.
insights.locator: That increased activity has led him to raise his forecasts

insights.claim: With no resolution to the Middle East conflict in sight, autumn 2027 budgeting may push more boards to commit to higher activity.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Watch Q4 budget guidance from E&Ps for confirmation of the capex pivot.
insights.locator: As companies enter the autumn budgeting season

insights.claim: Before the war, Wood Mackenzie expected a well-supplied market as OPEC+ unwound cuts, with Brent possibly falling to $50-$60; if the war ends and Hormuz traffic normalises, those conditions could return once global inventories are rebuilt.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: The current price spike has a plausible downside reversion path, so the risk premium is conditional on Hormuz.
insights.locator: Before the war, Wood Mackenzie was projecting

insights.claim: The UAE's decision to leave OPEC and Venezuela's industry revival as international investment returns add uncertainty, but next year's higher US Lower 48 output is likely to push global prices down, so US tight oil can play a swing-like role given time.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Additional supply from the UAE outside OPEC, Venezuela and the US points to a more bearish 2027 supply balance.
insights.quote: The US tight oil industry may not be an immediate swing producer, but given time it can play something like that role.
insights.locator: There are other factors complicating the outlook

insights.claim: Devon Energy is selling its Eagle Ford assets to Crescent Energy for $4.2 billion after its $58 billion merger with Coterra, with Wood Mackenzie calling the assets firmly non-core and the price broadly in line with its valuation; Crescent, already second-largest in the play, sees $140 million a year of synergies.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Post-merger portfolio pruning feeds consolidation of basin leaders like Crescent in the Eagle Ford.
insights.locator: Devon Energy has announced a deal to rationalise its portfolio

insights.claim: TotalEnergies CEO Patrick Pouyanné says disruption creates opportunities for companies with assets, and that vertical integration has turned European refineries, once seen as liabilities, into goldmines this year.
insights.speaker: Patrick Pouyanné, quoted by Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Refining margins from the diesel squeeze favour integrated majors with European downstream exposure.
insights.quote: I prefer the world of disruption to the peaceful world. There are more opportunities, but you need to have the assets.
insights.locator: Quote of the week

themes.theme: European power outlook and other WoodMac views

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's Strategic Planning Outlook expects European renewable power generation, across the EU, UK and Norway, to keep rising for many years through 2060 despite current headwinds.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: A long-run renewables build-out in Europe persists despite the energy crisis, supporting grid and storage investment.
